name: speech-tools
desc: C++ speech software library from the University of Edinburgh
why: Edinburgh speech toolkit from the Festival era is an old-school door into speech synthesis internals, though mostly library plumbing.

brief.what_it_is: Edinburgh Speech Tools is a C++ library of classes, functions and utility programs for speech software, from the University of Edinburgh's Centre for Speech Technology. It compiles to a single Unix .a library that other programs link against. It covers speech and linguistic classes (waveforms, tracks, labels), signal processing, audio playback and recording, and machine-learning helpers such as CART trees (wagon), n-grams, WFSTs and PCFGs. Its roughly 30 executables are thin command-line wrappers that read options and files, then call into the library. The homepage is the Doxygen API index for version 2.4.0, and the upstream README describes version 2.5.1.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the library holds C++ classes and functions that are frequently used in speech software, so that people do not duplicate effort. The authors also say that releasing code like this is meant to prevent that duplication.
brief.how_it_works: The source tree is split into speech_class, ling_class, sigpr, utils and audio sub-libraries, with a main directory whose minimal main() functions build the executables. The algorithms live in the libraries, and the programs only handle command-line options and file I/O. The README also says the SIOD Scheme interpreter and Festival-era pieces are included under their own licence terms.
brief.install_notes: The README points to an INSTALL file, which I did not fetch, so the build steps are unverified. The library builds with the shared make rules in config/. Audio support is aimed at the Network Audio system, Suns, and Linux and FreeBSD, so playback and recording (na_play, na_record) may depend on those. Building the full library documentation needs DOC++, JADE and docbook, which the README calls obscure, and it recommends using the pre-built documentation instead. I did not check the Homebrew formula, so nothing is known about its build options.
brief.standout: It is a plain library rather than an app: one .a file, with each executable as a thin main() over the same code. It also bundles a Scheme interpreter (SIOD) and a CART tree builder (wagon) from the Festival toolchain, which makes it an unusual window into how older speech synthesis systems were built.
brief.status: quiet. The README gives version 2.5.1 dated July 2020, and the homepage's Doxygen API index was generated Dec 2014 for 2.4.0. The README also says the docs are not up to date and are being moved to Doxygen. I could not see commit dates, so I cannot confirm recent activity.
brief.caveats: Licence: a permissive, BSD-like licence with conditions, including that authors' names may not be used to endorse products. Some files carry other licences: wfst_train.cc is Carnegie Mellon, SIOD and editline have their own terms, RXP is free for non-commercial use, and the README says none fall under the GPL. The README says parts of the release are incomplete or missing, and that newer parts have not been rigorously tested. The library docs are out of date. Audio code targets older platforms. The homepage shows only the API index, with no prose on usage.
quotes: The Edinburgh speech tools system is a library of C++ classes, functions and utility programs that are frequently used in speech software.
The system compiles to a single unix library .a file which can be linked with software.
Substantial parts of this release are considered mature and should be relatively free of bugs, however there are newer parts which have not rigourously tested yet.
Note the documentation is not up to date. We are in the process of moving the documentation to Doxygen.
